sentences.text: Mauriciosaurus was described in 2017 based on a single well-preserved juvenile specimen approximately 2 meters long.
This animal was a short-necked plesiosaur with a drop-shaped body and a small tail.
Each side of the upper jaw contained at least 42 teeth, comprising 4 in the premaxilla and 32 in the maxilla.
Dark grey, rectangular structures found in the type specimen likely represent scale-like tubercles that covered the underside of the creature's body.
The vertebrae of Mauriciosaurus have constricted outer surfaces, distinguishing them from the cylindrical vertebrae of Trinacromerum.
The coracoid bone of Mauriciosaurus lacks perforations along its midline and back margin, unlike those found in Dolichorhynchops and Trinacromerum.
The animal possessed flexible trailing edges on its flippers that acted as hydrofoils and a body outline shaped by contour fat merging the torso and tail.

Researchers interpret preserved soft tissue in Mauriciosaurus as a peritoneum richly pigmented by melanocytes, a heavily pigmented lining that likely protected the animal's internal organs from UV exposure.
The only known specimen of Mauriciosaurus was discovered in the summer of 2011 by workers at a quarry near Vallecillo in Nuevo León, Mexico.
The specimen was formally described in 2017 by Eberhard Frey, Eric Mulder, Wolfgang Stinnesbeck, Héctor Rivera Sylva, José Padilla Gutiérrez, and Arturo González González.
Mauriciosaurus likely hunted small prey because it had a slender snout and small, pointed teeth.
Researchers interpret preserved soft tissue in Mauriciosaurus as a peritoneum richly pigmented by melanocytes.
In modern desert or high-altitude squamates, peritoneal pigmentation protects reproductive organs from solar ultraviolet radiation, a function hypothesized for Mauriciosaurus.
Subcutaneous adipose tissue likely streamlined the body of Mauriciosaurus, similar to marine mammals.
Small neural spines and weak tail muscles suggest the preserved soft tissue cone on Mauriciosaurus's tail was contour fat used for stabilization, similar to fat-tailed geckos.
Frey et al. hypothesize that thick contour fat in plesiosaurs like Mauriciosaurus explains the rarity of preserved skin in the group.
Mauriciosaurus fell into soft, water-soaked, anoxic sediment at temperatures between 21 and 37 degrees Celsius, conditions that preserved its skin.
Anoxic conditions allowed subcutaneous fat to turn into adipocere, preserving the skin on the dorsal half of Mauriciosaurus's body.
Exposed parts of Mauriciosaurus's belly decayed before burial, causing the body cavity and gastralia to collapse.
Mauriciosaurus is a genus of polycotylid plesiosaur that lived in Mexico during the Late Cretaceous.
Biostratigraphic analysis dates the slab containing Mauriciosaurus to the early Turonian portion of the Agua Nueva Formation.
Mauriciosaurus is the first known juvenile polycotylid preserved in an environment other than shallow water.
Several unique features separate Mauriciosaurus from all other polycotylids, justifying its classification as a distinct genus.
